evidence: Ter. Ad. 2.2.28: jamne ēnumerāstī id, quod ad tē reditūrum putēs? (Lewis & Short)

phrases.english: Told to count, he counted six.
I’m counting to three: one … two … don’t make me say three!

phrases.latin: Age age, absolve mē atque argentum numerā, nē comitēs morer. — Pernumerātumst.
phrases.english: Come on, come on, settle up with me and count out the money, so I don’t keep my friends waiting. — It’s all counted out.

phrases.latin: Age, nummōs tuōs numerēmus: ūnus, duo, trēs …
phrases.english: Come on, let’s count your coins: one, two, three …

phrases.latin: Nunc contrā: ā decem ad ūnum. Decem, novem, octō …
phrases.english: Now the other way: from ten down to one. Ten, nine, eight …

phrases.latin: seu quia tot digitī, per quōs numerāre solēmus, … seu quod adūsque decem numerō crēscente venītur
phrases.english: either because there are that many fingers, on which we usually count, … or because the count rises all the way to ten

sources: Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 297.
